lesson_title: Day 6 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 5 (Day 5 lessons and the Tron lab: exchanges, VASPs, a permissioned-ledger freeze, deposit addresses and Energy)

lectures.title: Tron lab: sweeps, Energy and the USDT blacklist
Tron lab: who signs a deposit and its sweep
Exchanges, OTC desks and P2P markets

questions.question_stem: In the Tron lab's worked example, a deposit address sweeps its whole USDT balance to one wallet, and each sweep burns 13.3959 TRX for Energy. Who supplied that TRX?
questions.correct_answer: A separate account sent the TRX to the deposit address 10 to 15 minutes before each sweep.
incorrect_answers: The depositor, who attached the TRX to the same transfer that brought the USDT to the address.
The receiving wallet, which paid the sweep from its own balance when the USDT arrived there.
Nobody, because a sweep that moves a whole balance is free of any Energy charge on Tron.
questions.explanation: The sweep itself cost Energy, and the address had none, so it burned the TRX it held. A third account, not the depositor and not the receiver, topped the address up before each sweep (624, 864 and 894 seconds ahead). That outside payer is part of the deposit-address pattern.

questions.question_stem: A second Tron address makes 13 whole-balance sweeps, each using 64,285 Energy and burning 0 TRX, the Energy delegated from another account. Compared with the worked example, what does that show?
questions.correct_answer: Someone lent it Energy by staking TRX behind it, so a third party still pays for the sweeps.
incorrect_answers: The address owner staked their own TRX, so the owner and the sweep target are one party.
The sweeps were free because the balances were small, so no one paid anything for them.
The sweeps did not happen, because a transfer that burns no TRX is not recorded on Tron.
questions.explanation: In the worked example a payer sent TRX and the sweep burned it. Here the payer lent Energy, so nothing is burned. Either way, someone other than the address pays for its sweeps. Nothing in the record says who controls the lender's TRX either.

questions.question_stem: That second address was funded by 12 senders and swept to one address that no published source names. What confidence fits calling it a custodial deposit address?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate at most, and more often Low, because the pattern fits but no source ties the destination to a service.
incorrect_answers: High, because the sweeps match the worked example's pattern, which was already shown to be a deposit address there too.
None can be given, because the chain holds no evidence of any kind about how an address behaves or who pays for it.
Moderate, because 12 separate senders count as 12 independent kinds of evidence for the one same service they use.
questions.explanation: Many senders, whole-balance sweeps to one address and a third party paying each sweep repeat the worked example. Nothing names the destination, so the label is a pattern only. The 12 senders are one kind of evidence, repeated; High needs independent kinds.

questions.question_stem: The Tron lab shows two wallets blacklisted by the USDT contract. Which detail must a sentence about their current status carry?
questions.correct_answer: The block and time of the read, because the contract answers for the present only and a later read could differ.
incorrect_answers: The name of each wallet's owner, because the contract stores it beside each blacklist entry that it holds.
The date of the freeze alone, because a wallet that is blacklisted stays blacklisted for good once the issuer adds it.
The fee paid for the freeze, because it shows which agency asked the issuer to act on those two wallets.
questions.explanation: The AddedBlackList events are fixed on the chain (block 82,092,618, 23 Apr 2026), but whether a wallet is still blacklisted, and its balance, is read from the contract at a moment. The lab states both as of block 87,600,650. Who owns the wallets and why comes from sources, not from the chain.

questions.question_stem: In the Tron lab's worked example, 400 USDT reaches the deposit address from its depositor. Who signed that transfer, and who paid its fee?
questions.correct_answer: The depositor signed it and, having no Energy, burned TRX for the fee; the deposit address signed nothing.
incorrect_answers: The deposit address signed it and paid the fee from its own TRX, so the depositor was never involved.
The exchange signed it and lent the Energy, so no TRX was burned and the fee cost the depositor nothing at all.
The depositor signed it, and the USDT contract paid the fee in Energy that it holds for all holders.
questions.explanation: A transfer is signed by its sender. The depositor called the USDT contract, had no Energy and so burned 13.3959 TRX (31,895 Energy used; 13.7409 TRX fee in all). The deposit address only receives; it signs nothing for that transfer.

questions.question_stem: A customer deposits coins at an exchange, and a week later a withdrawal reaches another address. What can the chain show about the link between the two?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing: withdrawals are paid from the exchange's pooled wallets, so only the exchange's own records can pair them.
incorrect_answers: That the withdrawal came from the customer's deposit address, because each customer's coins stay in that address.
That they are linked whenever the amounts match, because the exchange pays a withdrawal from the coins just deposited.
That the deposit address signs the withdrawal, which is why exchange withdrawals show the customer as sender.
questions.explanation: Deposit addresses are per customer, but the exchange sweeps them into its own wallets and pays withdrawals from the pool. The chain cannot link a deposit to a later withdrawal; the exchange's ledger can.

specific_source.reading: Withdrawals come from the pool, not the deposit

questions.question_stem: On Bitcoin, an exchange sweep spends many recent deposits in one transaction. How do you cluster those inputs?
questions.correct_answer: Into the exchange's cluster, never into any one customer: the exchange has control of the coins, not ownership.
incorrect_answers: Into the customer whose deposit is largest, because the biggest input is the one that paid the fee and so owns it.
Into every depositor's cluster, because inputs spent together always belong to one customer's wallet or another one.
Not at all, because a sweep is a CoinJoin and its inputs are unrelated to each other, so no cluster forms at all, ever.
questions.explanation: Co-spending shows common control. Here the controller is the exchange, which holds the keys to every deposit address, so the inputs merge into its cluster and not into a customer's.

specific_source.reading: On Bitcoin, a sweep gathers many deposits

questions.question_stem: FinCEN's Section 311 final rule on Huione took effect on 17 November 2025. What does the rule do?
questions.correct_answer: It bars U.S. banks from holding correspondent accounts for Huione and from allowing indirect access.
incorrect_answers: It freezes Huione's addresses on the blockchain, so that coins held at those addresses can no longer move.
It places Huione on OFAC's SDN list, so that every U.S. person must block all of the firm's property.
It orders Huione to register as a money services business with FinCEN within the next 180 days.
questions.explanation: A Section 311 action acts on U.S. financial institutions' accounts. It is not an OFAC designation and does not freeze coins on chain: funds reaching Huione are a risk signal to report with a confidence word.

specific_source.reading: Huione: what the rule does and doesn't do

questions.question_stem: What does a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filed by an exchange give an analyst?
questions.correct_answer: A lead to follow with other evidence, not a finding that the activity was criminal.
incorrect_answers: A finding of fact, because an exchange files only once it has proved the activity illicit.
A confirmed owner for each address, because the report includes the customer's KYC file.
A confirmed attribution, because the exchange attests that its records name the owner.
questions.explanation: A SAR records what the exchange saw and suspected. It points you to records and addresses worth checking; it does not settle who did what.

specific_source.reading: The BSA makes the business keep records

questions.question_stem: Anyone can read Tron, yet USDT held on Tron can be frozen. Who can freeze it?
questions.correct_answer: The owner of the USDT contract, a multisignature wallet, through its blacklist functions; the 27 block producers cannot.
incorrect_answers: The 27 Super Representatives, who can blacklist any address by a vote when they produce a block of their own.
The account that delegated Energy to the address, which can freeze a balance by taking its Energy back at will.
Any exchange that has swept the address, since a sweep passes on the right to freeze that balance to the exchange.
questions.explanation: USDT on Tron uses the same TetherToken design as on Ethereum, with owner-only blacklist functions. The Super Representatives produce blocks but do not hold the contract's owner role. A freeze is true only as of the block you read. The owner is a multisignature wallet as of 31 Oct 2026; an owner can change.

specific_source.reading: USDT on Tron: same freeze, same owner rule

questions.question_stem: In the Tron lab's worked example, the deposit address sweeps its whole USDT balance to Binance's wallet. Whose key signed each sweep?
questions.correct_answer: The deposit address's own key, which the exchange holds; neither the depositor nor the payer signs it.
incorrect_answers: The depositor's key, because whoever paid the USDT in must also sign to send it on to the exchange.
The receiving wallet's key, because a Tron sweep is a pull that the wallet it goes to signs itself.
The key of whichever account paid for the sweep, because the account that pays a fee also signs.
questions.explanation: A transfer is signed by its sender, and the sweep's sender is the deposit address. The exchange holds that address's key, so the customer never signs from it. Paying for a transaction does not make an account its signer.

specific_source.reading: A deposit address is one customer's door
